messages.subject: Re: Ambar warning
messages.body_plain:
Dear List,

=20

I=B4m trying to analized some data using distance. My sample is a bit =
small, I

just have 46 observation of monkey clusters. I run the program using as =
a

model definition Half-normal/cosine. The run generated a warning that =
said:

Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. I don't really

understand why, but I suspect could be because the small sample size, it =

is
possible?=20

=20

Thanks for your patience.

=20

Natalia

=20

=20

-----Mensaje original-----
De: Wildlife abundance estimation using distance sampling techniques.
[mailto:DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK] En nombre de Steve Buckland
Enviado el: Mi=E9rcoles, 17 de Mayo de 2006 03:11 p.m.
Para: DISTANCE...@JISCMAIL.AC.UK
Asunto: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Line transects for sparrows

=20

I wonder if it is possible to put lines perpendicular to these features? =

If necessary, cut a narrow strip, cutting across the habitat types.  =
That=20

way, habitat type won't be correlated with distance from the line.

=20

Steve Buckland

=20

On Wed, 17 May 2006, Scott Somershoe wrote:

=20

> > Distance lovers:

> >    I'm working up protocol for surveying breeding Henslow Sparrows in

> > Tennessee.  They are secretive grassland birds, but sing regularly and

> > can be surveyed adequately with line transects.  I have several fields

> > where they breed, but I have a technical problem I have to deal with =
in

> > order to conduct surveys without violating assumptions of distance

> > sampling.  The main problem is that some fields are narrow (~50m or

> > less), where we can only do one-sided transects where we walked the

> > transect line as the edge between mowed and unmowed habitat.  I'm ok

> > with one-sided transects.  I think I can deal with surveying narrow

> > habitats.

> >   To build up to the question, I think I'm going to run a series of

> > one-sided transects at our 3 sites, which will deal with the narrow

> > habitat issue.  The problem is that 2 large fields (300m x ~400m) have =
a

> > lot of firebreaks mowed lengthwise thru the field.  Essentially there

> > are several 15-25m wide strips of "suitable" habitat (with standing =
dead

> > native warm season grasses) that stretch the length of the field and

> > then there's a 10m wide strip of growing blackberry and other greenery

> > not so suitable for Henslow's, repeat for 300m.  I'm sure HESP's =
forage

> > in the greenery/firebreaks, but would not necessarily use it for

> > nesting.  To add to the plot, HESP's are found in large fields of =
almost

> > exclusively green grasses that were burned the previous year (not

> > expected to be optimal habitat).  So maybe the firebreaks aren't =
really

> > a series issue.  My question is how to deal with the firebreaks and

> > unsuitable nesting habitat scattered between lines of suitable =
habitat?

> > Doing a point count isn't really the way to go for surveying these =
guys,

> > but a line transect would survey ample suitable and unsuitable =
habitat,

> > thus on a given transect, there would never be detections from 15-25m =
on

> > the length of the transect.  Also, if we worked line transects, =
walking

> > the edge of the mowed/ummowed grasses would be best, but I'm not sure =
if

> > we violate assumptions of distance sampling because there may be no =
HESP

> > along the transect line.  Thus we would technically get all the birds

> > along the line, but that is because there may not be any.

> >=20

> > Thoughts would be greatly appreciated.

> >=20

> > Thanks,

> > Scott Somershoe

> >=20

messages.subject: Re: Ambar warning
messages.body_plain:
Natalia-

This is a warning but does not necessarily mean that there is a problem=20
with the analysis.  The phrase

Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity.

is referring to the adjustment cosine functions and they are being=20
constrained such that the detection function can only be flat or=20
decrease from x=3D0 to x=3DW.  This is called "monotone non-increasing"=20
where monotone means the "same throughout" so the function never=20
increases higher than at x=3D0.

The function may want to increase for several reasons. 1) with a small=20
sample and the randomization of locations, more animals may have just=20
happen to be located far from the line than closer to it, 2) animals may=20
have moved away from the line before they were detected, 3) heaping=20
(rounding) of distance measurements to convenient values, or 4) the data=20
may need to be truncated because it is trying to add many adjustments to=20
fit a long tail.  There may be others that I've not thought of now.

You are the best judge to determine which situation applies for your=20
data.  It may be that with some judicious right truncation that deletes=20
a few data points that you can fit a better detection function if you=20
have some observations that are well into the tail.  But it may be one=20
of the other reasons.

regards,

Jeff

messages.body_plain:
Workshop: Introduction to Distance Sampling
University of Auckland, New Zealand
28th - 30th June 2006

A reminder that 16 June is the last date for registration for the above
workshop to avoid a late registration charge.
You may register on-line at http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/NZ2006/NZ.html

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

Introduction to Distance Sampling

This 3-day workshop will give participants a solid grounding in the basic
methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys for estimating
the density and/or abundance of wildlife populations. It is a blend of
theory and practice, and participants will learn how to use the industry-
standard program Distance.  We will focus on "conventional" distance
sampling methods, as described in the standard reference book "Introduction
to Distance Sampling".

The workshop is aimed at wildlife managers, ecologists and statisticians.
It features a mix of lectures and hands-on computer sessions.  It will be
taught by Steve Buckland and David Borchers from the Centre for Research
into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) at St Andrews, and by
Rachel Fewster from the Department of Statistics at the University of
Auckland.

I think there are a lot of free extensions and tools available at ESRI's
website. Search for "distance and azimuth" at http://arcscripts.esri.com/=

calculating new coordinates on a 3D surface of a geographic coordinate

e a
suitable projection. Moreover I think as distance measurement units are
rather small (i.e. meters, rarely kilometers) in comparison to the extent=
 of
your entire survey area, so errors due to projecting your coordinates wil=
l
be acceptable (in general distance measurement errors will be larger than=

projection errors). If you are using ArcView check the web site mentioned=

r
unprojected observer positions (on the transect) from a dbase file, conve=
rt
the coordinates to a different projection (optional), and compute object
positions based on the projectd coordinates, distances, and (geographic)
angles stored in the attribute table.

Hope this helps and best regards

=09Felix

messages.subject: Re: N vs Nb
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 19 Jun 2006, Daniel Pike wrote:

> > I am running some analyses where the bootstrap N (Nb) is sometimes up

> > to twice as large as the simple N estimate.  I understand that Nb is the

> > mean of all the bootstrap re-samplings. But I am not clear about what

> > circumstances would lead to such a large difference between N and Nb. It

> > seems to me that they should be similar. I am also not clear about which

> > one is more appropriate for use under these circumstances.

Daniel, Distance outputs the man bootstrap estimate on the bootstrap
summary page.  If individual bootstrap estimates are up to double the
original estimate, this isn't a problem, though it indicates high
variance.  If the mean is double the original estimate, then that is a
problem.  You shouldn't use the bootstrap estimate, though it can be used
to correct the original estimate for bias.  I don't do this because the
bias adjustment can have very high variance, so it can make your estimate
worse in terms of root mean square error.  In your case, the bias-adjusted
estimate is likely to be too small - possibly even negative!

I don't know why you're getting this ... possibly you have too few lines
to make reliable use of the bootstrap, and a high proportion of your
detections are from a single line?  I would not use the bootstrap if you
have less than around 12 lines, and I would prefer at least 20.  If most
of your detections are from just 2 or 3 lines, again I would not use the
bootstrap.  The nonparametric bootstrap performs very badly if you
have small numbers of lines or your detections are concentrated on a
small proportion of lines.

Steve

messages.subject: Re: Multipliers
messages.body_plain:
Barbara and List:

A glance at the Distance Users Manual discusses the topic of multipliers
in Chapter 8 (Conventional distance sampling).  In the section entitled
"Additional uses of multipliers" the common/rare species use of
multipliers as you are describing is defined.  You will note that the
model definition to use in fitting the detection function is the uniform
with no adjustment terms; and specify the multiplier in the Multiplier
tab.  The detection function fitted by Distance will produce a
probability of detection of 1.0, and the estimated density will
incorporate the multiplier you specified.

By specifying a detection function model other than the uniform with no
adjustment term, you are defeating the purpose of providing your
multiplier.  Because of the few detections of your rare species, you are
requesting that a detection function *not* be fit to the data for that
species, and the multiplier (and SE) you provide will perform the
function of specifying detectability.

I hope that helps clarify your dilemma.

messages.subject: Re: Multipliers
messages.body_plain:
Hi Barbara, list:

Further to Eric's message, in the online manual's program reference, under
Multipliers Tab - CDS and MCDS, is the text below.  If you didn't find it then
other probably didn't either, so I've moved it to the Users Guide instead.

 - Len

Aside: In fact, the Distance Analysis Engine only recognizes the multiply
operator - i.e., all multipliers multiply the density estimate.  So, the
Distance Interface uses a little trick to pass multipliers to the Analysis
Engine when the operator is divide.  To pass the multiplier value, it simply
takes 1 / multiplier value.  To pass the multiplier SE, it takes SE /
(multiplier value * multiplier value).  You can see this happening if you look
at the first page of the Analysis Details Results tab for an analysis that has
been run with multipliers, where the operator is a divider.  About half-way
down the first page is a small table listing the multiplier values and SEs
used.  If, for example, you used a multiplier with a value of 0.9 and an SE of
0.5, you'll see that the actual value passed in was 1.1 (i.e., 1 / 0.9) and
the SE was 0.6128 (i.e., 0.5 / (0.9*0.9) ).

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator, Distance Development Project

messages.subject: Re: Primate census
messages.body_plain:
Hi Natalia, list:

There are several problems with your design.

Firstly, you surveyed from established tracks.  This raises two issues.  (i)
density along tracks is unlikely to be the same as average density in the
whole national park, so you can only make inferences about density in the
area you survyved, not the whole park; (ii) if density of animals is
affected by distance from track (e.g., they use the tracks) then the
assumption used in estimating the detection function that true density is
uniform with respect to perpendicular distance is incorrect, so you get a
biased estimate of detection probability and so a biased estimate of
density, even along the tracks. You should locate transects at random
(preferrably systematic random) throughout the study area of interest and if
you must cut the lines use minimal cutting.  See chapter 7 of the
Introduction to Distance Sampling book for lots more on this (particuarly
sections 7.8.3 on repeat transects, 7.8.4 on cut transects and 7.8.5 on the
use of paths).

Secondly you only surveyed 2 transects.  This is not enough to give you a
reliable estimate of the spatial variation in density, which is usually a
major component of the overall variance estimate.  So, the CVs you have
obtained are very unrealiable.  When you survey the same line many times,
you should pool all detections from the same lines together at the analysis
stage (and multiply line length by the number of visits) - you then have a
sample size of 2 transects for estimating variation in encounter rate
between transects, not 24.  This has been covered a few times in previous
posts to this list (check the archives, which are searchable).  You probably
missed the bit in the book about recommended minimum sample size of
transects - in section 7.2.1 they recommend 10-20, and I'd go for 20 over
10!

You asked about comparing the results with those of someone who measured
perpendicular distance to the first animal of the cluster rather than the
center.  You did the correct thing (see pages 119 and 272 of the book);
their method will produce an upward bias in the density estimate.

In my experience, there is a great deal of poor practice in both field and
analysis methods in the primate survey literature.  I don't know why this
is, but you certainly need to be careful when comparing your results to
those of others.

I hope this helps,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Aquatic birds
messages.body_plain:
Dear list,

=20

I=B4m trying to calculate density of aquatic birds in rice fields with =
different growing stages (I'll call them "habitats"). There are several =
questions I am trying to solve, however, some of some issues remain =
unclear to me.

=20

The survey was carried out using point transects of 500 meters between =
points. With an irregular number of points per transect and in some =
cases there are complete points and other are half points (this is =
solved with the point effort at the points).  Distances were measures =
using regular intervals of 10 m up to 150 m (grouped data).

=20

1) There are only 10 species with more than 30 observations when pooling =
the data for two countries and post- stratifying them by habitat. It is =
right to post stratify like this?

=20

2) The people who did the survey told me that they took into account =
birds before they flew away, however, I have run the analysis for =
several species and the first intervals have less individuals (if not =
any) compared to distances out to about 100 m. In some of the analysis =
the GOF test is low and I don't realize which model I must choose...

How can I realize if this is a situation of evasive movement of birds o =
if it is due to the nature of point transect data at low distances? Do I =
have to left-truncate?=20

I've read Chapter 5  related to this in Buckland et al. 2001, but I was =
wondering if others have experiences with similar problems and if anyone =
has suggestions regarding analysis of these data.

=20

Thank you!

=20

Andrea.
